pullRequest.title: Refreshable tokens: review fixes across the stack
pullRequest.bodyHTML:
Description

This is a follow-up to the refreshable (short-lived) OAuth token stack (#14450 through #14456). It collects the fixes made in response to review feedback on those PRs into a single branch on top of the stack tip (#14456), so the series history stays readable while the fixes land together.

Because the feedback spanned every PR in the stack, the changes here touch the public HTTP client, the config storage layer, the auth login/refresh/token/status flows, the git credential helper path, agent-task and CAPI per-request refresh, and the guided verification scripts. None of it changes the externally documented behavior of the feature; it corrects edge cases, concurrency safety, and backward compatibility that surfaced during review.

The sections below explain each commit. They are grouped by the PR in the stack that the feedback came from.

Changes

Foundation (#14450)

fix(api): keep public HTTP client token config backward compatible (9c664a5)
The exported api seam no longer speaks the internal gh types. The primitive config interface keeps its original shape (ActiveToken(string) (string, string) plus HostForAPIHost) and AddAuthTokenHeader keeps its original signature, so existing downstream consumers compile unchanged. Refresh now lives on a separate, refresh-aware seam: HTTPClientOptions gains two mutually exclusive fields, the primitive Config and a new RefreshingConfig, and the credential and refresh types move to a new public pkg/auth package. Regression tests cover the primitive path.

test(config): pin intentional active-token lookup behavior (1844179)
ActiveToken has one narrow state that diverges from older gh (per-user config oauth_token, no per-user keyring slot, an unkeyed keyring token present, no host-level oauth_token). This change keeps the new, more correct behavior as the groundwork for the refreshable per-user slot, adds a code comment explaining why that state is rare in practice, and pins it with a test so it is not later mistaken for a regression.

Domain (#14451)

fix(config): purge refreshable record on non-refreshable login (739aa72)
A plain Login used to leave a stale refreshable record behind, so a user could hold both a refreshable and a non-expiring credential at once. Login now removes the user's refreshable record (both keyring and config forms) before completing, mirroring what loginRefreshable already does in reverse, so activateUser falls through to the non-expiring path and copies the new token into the host-level oauth_token slot that go-gh reads for extensions.

fix(config): align TokenForUser precedence with setActiveCredential (6ea35dd)
TokenForUser now checks the refreshable credential first, then the non-refreshable keyring token, then the non-refreshable config token, matching setActiveCredential, so activation and resolution can never disagree about which credential is current even if a mixed state ever slips through. The purge above makes that state unreachable in normal flows, but keeping the order identical is cheap insurance.

Login, refresh, and git credential helper (#14452)

fix(auth refresh): avoid printing short-lived downgrade warning twice (5676a41)
The post-completion summary no longer repeats the "Original token was short-lived; pass --short-lived to preserve it" line. It is still printed once up front, before the browser prompt, so the user can abort early.

fix(auth refresh): preserve scopes when refreshing an expired refreshable token (f4f010f)
With the old ActiveToken read, refreshing a credential whose access token had already expired handed back the stale token, so GetScopes got a 401 and the refreshed credential came back with no scopes. The refresh now uses ActiveTokenWithRefresh, so the token is renewed and persisted first and scopes are read off a live token. When scopes genuinely cannot be read, it prints a non-blocking stderr warning telling the user to re-add scopes with --scopes rather than failing the whole refresh.

fix(auth/shared): offer to set up gh when a non-gh helper meets a refreshable token (4840e2e)
When the auth flow returns a refreshable token and a non-gh credential helper is configured, gh now explains the problem and offers to set itself up as the helper for the host. Accepting lets gh refresh the token transparently; declining keeps the previous behavior of rejecting the existing credential and warning. This prompt lives at the post-auth setup step because that is the earliest point where both facts are known (the token is refreshable and the helper is non-gh).

fix(auth/shared): force web flow for short-lived interactive login (669ab0c)
A pasted personal access token can never be refreshable, so --short-lived now forces the web flow and no longer offers the "Paste an authentication token" choice.

fix(auth/shared): clarify warning when declining gh helper setup (e47b82d)
The reject warning now states that the credential was not stored and that git operations may prompt or fail on the next attempt, rather than framing it as a failure only after expiry. This branch is now only reached when the user declines the new setup prompt above.

refactor(authflow): extract authResultFromToken for test coverage (870382c)
The mapping from the OAuth flow result to AuthResult now lives in authResultFromToken, tested directly for both responses: with refresh metadata (refreshable credential populated, expiry anchored at the request instant) and without (plain token, Refreshable nil).

gh auth token (#14453)

refactor(auth/token): drop redundant RefreshStatusDone check under --secure-storage (6c1e258)
RefreshStatusDone is only ever produced after validation that requires a non-empty refresh token, so the credential already satisfies IsRefreshable() by then. The || refreshStatus == gh.RefreshStatusDone disjunct was dead code; the condition is simplified to cred.IsRefreshable() with no behavior change.

fix(auth/token): restore legacy unkeyed keyring lookup when --user is omitted (de38197)
The non-refreshable keyring fallback was keyed on the resolved active username, so when only the legacy unkeyed keyring slot existed but an active user was recorded, it read the empty per-user slot and reported no token found. It now keys the fallback on the --user flag value, so omitting --user reads the legacy unkeyed slot exactly as the original --secure-storage behavior did. Pinned by two TestTokenRunSecureStorage states that fail against the pre-fix code.

gh auth status (#14454)

fix(auth/status): handle rejected refresh token without an empty-token request (f3a6412)
On a rejected refresh token the credential is removed during resolution, and the old code carried on with an empty token and sent the scope request with Authorization: token (nothing after it), surfacing a confusing generic failure. buildEntry now short-circuits on RefreshStatusExpired: it skips the scope request, sets a dedicated refresh_expired entry state, and prints a clear reason plus the re-authenticate instruction. The entry stays a non-success state, so gh auth status still exits non-zero and routes to stderr.

agent-task and CAPI (#14455)

test(agent-task/capi): assert per-request token refresh in CAPI transport (c13b3f4)
The existing tests supplied a fixed empty credential, so a regression back to a construction-time lookup would have passed unnoticed. A new client_test.go exercises the transport directly: one test wires a fake source returning a different token per call and asserts each freshly resolved token becomes that request's header, and another covers the best-effort behavior where the request still proceeds with the last stored token when refresh errors.

fix(agent-task): accept plaintext refreshable OAuth credentials (dab3377)
The agent-task preflight only recognized the oauth_token and keyring sources as device-flow logins. A short-lived login whose credential falls back to plaintext config is tagged refreshable_oauth_token, so the preflight rejected a supported account before the CAPI refresh path could run. The preflight now accepts the refreshable source alongside the other two.

Concurrency safety and robustness (config)

fix(config): run logout under the shared refresh lock (5c4be83)
Logout now runs its whole body under the same best-effort refresh lock a concurrent refresh uses, reloading fresh config first, so a logout racing an in-flight refresh cannot be undone by the refresher persisting a renewed credential after the user logged out. Logout wins in both interleavings.

fix(config): skip destructive refresh cleanup when the lock is unavailable (9f9121e)
When a refresh token is rejected, the dead credential is normally removed. Without the refresh lock a rejection is ambiguous: a peer process may have already spent the same single-use refresh token and be about to persist the renewed one, so deleting could discard the peer's valid credential. The destructive cleanup is now gated on actually holding the lock; skipping it is self-healing because the next invocation reads the peer's renewed credential.

fix(config): don't fail refresh when the config dir can't be created (3687fef)
Acquiring the refresh lock first ensures the config directory exists. If that creation fails (for example on a read-only filesystem), the refresh now degrades to running without the lock, exactly like a failed lock acquisition, instead of failing outright. The lock is already best effort, and if control reached a refresh the credential was already read, so proceeding is strictly better than erroring. The common case (an existing directory) is unaffected.

fix(config): run login under the shared refresh lock (24d96dd)
Login now runs its whole body under the same best-effort refresh lock that LoginRefreshable and Logout use, reloading fresh config first, so a plain login racing an in-flight refresh wins in both interleavings: a refresh that persists first is superseded by the credential stored here, and a refresh still waiting on the lock reloads afterwards, finds the refreshable record removed, and bails without resurrecting it. The lock stays best effort, so login still proceeds when it cannot be acquired. This commit also surfaces a genuine failure to purge the user's refreshable record during a non-refreshable login: a surviving record outranks the freshly stored token during activation, so a silently failed removal would let login report success while the stale credential stayed active. The check verifies the post-condition by re-reading rather than inspecting the delete error, so it stays silent in environments without a working keyring (an unavailable keyring resolves to not found) and only surfaces when a record provably survives removal.

Guided verification scripts (#14456) and housekeeping

docs(script): clarify refreshable-token e2e scripts (858cab7)
Reworded the script header to describe the scenarios inline instead of linking a note that never shipped, and removed an orphaned # NEW SYSTEM banner that had no counterpart.

fix(script): declare authtype capability in gitcredential e2e on git 2.46+ (940a11d)
Declaring capability[]=authtype on git 2.46 and newer makes the credential fill steps exercise the same path real fetch and push take, so gh marks the credential ephemeral and the step asserts ephemeral=1 deterministically instead of leaving it to the eye.

docs(script): prompt reviewer to confirm git auth during gitcredential e2e login (567cea4)
Added a bold reviewer-action note at the login step so the reviewer knows to confirm the "Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials?" prompt, which exercises the credential-helper setup path for the host.

chore: fix formatting (f7b5fbd)
gofmt struct-field alignment in api/client_test.go after the longer RefreshingConfig field name. No behavior change.

How did you test this change?

I rebuilt gh from this branch and ran both guided end-to-end verification scripts against a real host, confirming every scenario behaved as expected.

With script/refreshable-token-e2e.sh I walked through short-lived login, an ordinary command refreshing an expired token on demand, the GH_TOKEN environment path, and gh auth status both refreshing and with --no-refresh. Refreshes were confirmed from gh's GH_DEBUG=api request log and from auth status output. I ran this for both the secure keyring theme and the insecure config theme.

With script/refreshable-token-gitcredential-e2e.sh I set this build as my git credential helper and exercised resolving a credential, refreshing an expired one through git, and the warning path. My local git is 2.43, so this run exercised the older-git stale-helper warning path rather than the git 2.46 non-cacheable "ephemeral" attribute path.

Key points

The fixes are kept as focused, individually reviewable commits so each one can be read against the PR it responds to. The single-branch approach was chosen over amending each stacked PR in place to avoid repeatedly rewriting the history of the whole stack during review.

The guided e2e scripts carry testing-only env hacks (for example GH_AT_EXPIRES_IN) used to force expiry on demand. These are intentionally retained here so the scripts remain runnable, and will be removed in a dedicated wrap-up PR on top of this one.

Notes for reviewers

Start from the config storage changes in internal/config (config.go, refreshable.go), which carry the concurrency-safety and robustness fixes, then follow the per-area commits outward into the auth command packages.

This PR targets user-3/refresh-token-e2e (the tip of the stack, #14456), not trunk. Review it after the underlying stack.

Authorship and follow-up

Who wrote this:

  • A human wrote it.
  • An agent wrote it under close human direction.
  • An agent wrote it independently, and no human has guided the implementation beyond the initial prompt.

Who answers review comments:

  • @user-3 will read and reply directly.
  • An agent will draft replies and @user-3 will read them before they are posted.
  • Nobody has explicitly committed to replying.

nodes.bodyHTML: 🛑 Requirement: Make this credential-kind replacement atomic and verify that the purge succeeds. Login runs outside the refresh lock and discards failure from deleting the refreshable keyring record. A refresh already in flight can therefore re-persist its rotated record after this deletion, or a failed delete can leave the old record in place; because TokenForUser now prioritizes refreshable credentials, Login can report success while the old short-lived credential remains authoritative. Serialize the full replacement with refresh and propagate non-not-found purge failures before completing login.

nodes.bodyHTML: 🛑 Requirement: Do not perform logout's destructive write when the cross-process lock was not acquired. withFreshConfigForRefresh deliberately invokes this callback with lockHeld == false after a timeout or unsupported lock, but this callback ignores that signal. A peer refresh can then finish after logout and persist a renewed credential, undoing a logout that already returned success. Require serialization for logout, or use a conflict-safe retry/error path when the lock is unavailable.

🛑 Requirement: This message can falsely claim the credential was removed. The new lock-unavailable path intentionally leaves it stored, and even the lock-held cleanup ignores deletion/write failures. Report only that the credential can no longer be refreshed unless cleanup success is carried into the entry state.

🛑 Requirement: RefreshStatusExpired does not guarantee that storage cleanup succeeded: cleanup is skipped without the lock and its errors are ignored when attempted. This JSON error therefore exposes a false script-facing claim. Keep the error limited to the confirmed rejection unless the refresh API starts reporting cleanup success.

💭 Commentary: Answering this first prompt does not always configure gh. When a non-gh helper already exists, the new Setup branch asks a second confirmation before calling ConfigureOurs; declining it leaves gh unconfigured. Since this step is meant to exercise helper setup, tell the reviewer to accept the follow-up prompt too.

nodes.bodyHTML:
Food For Thought

Doing a keyring lookup here adds 30ms (on MacOS) for every API request, which in nearly all cases (since most people aren't using refreshable tokens) is totally unneeded.

Firstly, we should look into caching the token (non-blocking for this PR) but also, it seems really lame that every user is going to pay this extra cost for 1 request commands. Not really sure what to do about it except reverse the order here and in setActiveCredential to optimise for the more common case.

WDYT?
I think they take the lock now?

Concern

I don't think the ConfigDir is the right place to put the lock. All our nix home-manager friends (and similar projects) have immutable config dirs so locking is always going to fail.

nodes.bodyHTML:
Question

Just help me clarify my understanding.

Given I'm logged in with gh auth login --short-lived
And Given my setup can't take the lock (e.g. network mount)
And Given my refresh token is dead, because I revoked the app's authorization or it passed its ~6 month lifetime
And Given my access token has expired
When I run gh pr list
Then gh sends a refresh request with the dead token, and the server rejects it
And the credential stays stored, because lockHeld is false
And this request goes out with no token, which is a 401, or an anonymous call for public data
When I run any other gh command, or git uses gh as its credential helper
Then the same thing happens again: a refresh request is rejected and nothing changes in storage
And this repeats on every request until I run gh auth login

?

Yep, your walkthrough is correct. When we can't take the lock we leave the stored credential in place, so every subsequent request (including git going through gh as a credential helper) re-attempts the same doomed refresh, gets rejected, and resolves to no usable token, right up until the user re-authenticates. 👍

One precision on "goes out with no token": we don't send an empty token, we drop the Authorization header entirely. The rejection path returns an empty gh.Credential{}, and the round tripper only sets the header when the token is non-empty:

if token != "" {
    req.Header.Set(authorization, fmt.Sprintf("token %s", token))
}

So the request is genuinely header-less (anonymous), not Authorization: token with an empty value. That distinction matters because the empty-value form returns Bad credentials, whereas a header-less request returns Requires authentication (or an anonymous public-data response).

The small upside is that for REST endpoints the API response does hint at the failure: a 401 Requires authentication, which we follow with a Try authenticating with: ... line. One wrinkle there: because the now-useless credential is still stored and still looks refreshable, that hint currently points at gh auth refresh rather than gh auth login. It does still recover, since gh auth refresh re-runs the OAuth flow, but the wording is a little misleading given the refresh token is the dead part.

One caveat for completeness: GraphQL is less friendly, since an unauthenticated GraphQL request comes back as a 403 rate-limit (anonymous limit is 0), so the 401 hint never fires and the user just sees a rate-limit message with no pointer to re-auth.

My take: I think this edge case is fine to accept. It only bites users who haven't run gh for a long time, and there's a good chance they can self-correct from the messaging we already surface (and we could add similar messaging for failed GraphQL calls to tighten this further). The alternative, cleaning up the expired tokens (refresh plus auth) in this state, would reintroduce exactly the concurrency problem we were trying to avoid: racing refresh requests in an environment without flock support. And I suspect that concurrent case is only going to get more common as parallel working agents become a thing.

🟡 Changes recommended

Credential replacement and logout can still race refreshes, and rejected-token status can falsely claim successful cleanup.

5 open findings
  • Serialize credential replacement and propagate purge failures · New
  • Prevent logout writes when refresh lock is unavailable · New
  • Do not claim credential removal without confirmed cleanup · New
  • Avoid claiming refresh cleanup succeeded without confirmation · New
  • Ensure helper setup completes when an existing helper is present · New
What changed in this PR

This follow-up consolidates review fixes for the refreshable OAuth token stack across API clients, credential storage, authentication commands, and verification tooling.

Changes:

  • Restores public API compatibility while adding a separate refresh-aware client seam.
  • Refines credential precedence, refresh handling, logout synchronization, and authentication UX.
  • Expands regression tests and guided end-to-end verification.
